---
name: frontend-design
description: Build or revise product-specific web interfaces with design-system discipline and rendered verification. Use for HTML, CSS, JavaScript, or TypeScript frontend work including marketing pages, dashboards, forms, settings, authentication, components, empty states, and responsive UI.
---

# Frontend Design

Treat frontend design as a closed system: understand the product and its visual language before adding UI. Distinctiveness should come from product evidence, information hierarchy, and precise composition instead of generic decoration.

## Authority

Explicit user requirements and approved design specifications govern first. Existing project components and conventions govern next. Use this package's defaults only to fill gaps. Ask one focused question when those authorities conflict; never create a second visual language silently.

## 1. Detect the design context

Inspect relevant source before planning markup. Find theme and token files, typography and icon conventions, layout primitives, component libraries, nearby pages, and frontend validation scripts.

| Mode | Evidence | Response |
|---|---|---|
| Existing system | Several token and component categories are established | Reuse them |
| Partial system | Some visual conventions exist | Preserve them and fill only uncovered needs |
| Greenfield | No meaningful visual system exists | Define the smallest semantic token set and reusable primitives needed for this task |
| Ambiguous | Signals conflict | Ask which direction governs the work |

Continue only after recording the mode and the files that support it.

## 2. Select an archetype

Read [`../../standards/page-archetypes.md`](../../standards/page-archetypes.md) completely. Choose the closest archetype before implementation. A feature inside an established application normally uses the component or application-feature archetype unless it replaces an entire page.

The selection is complete when every required region or state is accounted for and genuinely inapplicable items are marked as such.

## 3. Define hierarchy and evidence

Use [`../../standards/task-brief.md`](../../standards/task-brief.md) to state the working contract:

```text
page purpose and user
primary task and primary action
optional secondary action
required content and section order
concrete product evidence
components and tokens to reuse
responsive behavior
accessibility requirements
```

Prefer a real product interface, then real data, code or terminal output, a technical or process diagram, and finally a product-specific illustration. When interface copy changes, read [`../../standards/content-standards.md`](../../standards/content-standards.md) completely before drafting it.

Move on when every section supports the primary task and the archetype's first viewport contains the required product evidence.

## 4. Establish implementation constraints

Read these files completely before changing frontend source:

- [`../../standards/frontend-standards.md`](../../standards/frontend-standards.md)
- [`../../standards/forbidden-patterns.md`](../../standards/forbidden-patterns.md)

An existing system owns component behavior and visual values. Use approved components with named variants. Treat shared design-system source and standards as protected during product UI work. If a required capability is missing, report the exact gap and ask before changing the design system or adding a one-off variant. In partial and greenfield systems, place new values in reusable semantic tokens rather than scattering raw values through feature code.

Implementation may begin once every component and visual value has an established source or one clearly defined new semantic source.

## 5. Build the smallest complete slice

Implement in reading order. Preserve semantic HTML and keyboard behavior. Keep focus visible and honor reduced-motion preferences. Cover each state the feature can enter, including disabled or selected behavior and any loading, empty, success, or error result. Keep action priority and content order intact as the viewport changes.

Motion should explain feedback or continuity. A card should mark a useful boundary or grouped interaction.

Finish this step only when the requested flow works through every applicable state and representative width.

## 6. Run repository checks

Run the actual frontend checks found in step 1. Exercise available linting and compilation, behavior tests, accessibility checks, and visual tests. Do not invent script names. Do not update visual baselines unless the task explicitly authorizes a reviewed baseline change.

Every available check must pass. For an unavailable category, record the evidence showing that the repository does not provide it.

## 7. Verify rendered output

Capture the affected interface with project browser tooling when possible. Otherwise use another available browser automation tool. Review these representative viewports:

```text
390 x 844
768 x 1024
1440 x 900
```

Inspect primary interactions and visible focus where practical. Read [`../../standards/visual-review-rubric.md`](../../standards/visual-review-rubric.md) completely, score the render, fix each critical failure and applicable violation, then capture the corrected result once.

When browser access is unavailable, apply the same rubric to source and state that rendered verification could not run. Completion requires a passing review or a concrete external blocker for every remaining failure.

## Completion report

State the archetype and context mode. Name reused or added system resources, the product evidence shown, every command and result, screenshot paths or the browser limitation, and any unresolved design-system capability or external blocker.

name: tdd
description: Test-driven development for behavior-bearing code. Use whenever TDD Guard is active, when building features or fixing bugs, or when the user requests test-first work, red-green development, or integration tests.
---

# Test-Driven Development

Work in vertical Red → Green slices. This skill defines test quality and workflow; the Pi extension and Probity enforce source writes at tool boundaries.

Read `CONTEXT.md` when present, relevant ADRs, project instructions, and nearby tests before choosing a seam or naming behavior.

## Choose a public seam

A seam is the public boundary where behavior can be observed without reaching into implementation details.

When an existing public seam is obvious, state it briefly and proceed. Ask the user before writing a test only when the contract is unclear or materially different seams would produce different designs, costs, or coverage.

Tests should remain valid when internals are refactored without changing behavior.

See [tests.md](tests.md) for examples and [mocking.md](mocking.md) for boundary guidance.

## Write tests worth keeping

A good test describes caller-visible behavior through a public interface. Its expected value comes from an independent source such as a worked example or known literal. It fails when behavior is absent or wrong, survives internal restructuring, and makes one logical behavioral claim.

Private-method tests, internal call assertions, and project-owned collaborator mocks couple the suite to implementation. Expected results that repeat the implementation calculation or compare a value to itself are tautological. Write one test, learn from its result, and then choose the next case.

## Run one vertical slice

**Red:** Add one behavior-driving test and run the narrow relevant command. Confirm the failure comes from the expected assertion or behavior mismatch. Failures during test loading or setup do not establish a clean red. When infrastructure prevents the assertion from running, add only the placeholder needed to reach it.

**Green:** Add the minimum production behavior required by the observed failure. Run the narrow test again, followed by the broader relevant suite. Start the next behavior with a new red test.

Do not write all tests first and implementation later. Each cycle is a tracer bullet informed by the previous result.

## Refactoring

Refactoring is optional review work, not a mandatory step between every Red → Green slice. Refactor only while relevant tests are green. Do not introduce new behavior during refactoring.

## Guard interaction

Use Pi's `edit` and `write` tools for source changes so Probity can inspect pending content. Do not mutate source through shell redirection, in-place editors, patch commands, inline scripts, or other bypasses.

A guard block is evidence that the pending write lacks a valid TDD justification. Address the named problem. Do not weaken the test, alter expected behavior to match broken code, disable the guard, or search for another write path.

Only the user may disable enforcement with `/tdd off` or authorize a specific exception in the conversation.

# Approved Page Archetypes

Select one archetype before implementation. Preserve its required regions unless the task makes one genuinely inapplicable.

## Marketing product page

Use for a homepage or major product overview.

```text
Navigation → left-aligned value proposition → one primary action → concrete product evidence → proof or technical credibility → workflow → major capabilities → installation or usage example → final action
```

The first viewport shows a product screenshot, code sample, real data, or technical diagram. Keep the headline concrete and let content determine hero height.

## Product-detail landing page

Use for one feature, integration, or use case.

```text
Product context → specific problem → specific mechanism → product evidence → workflow → constraints or compatibility → proof → action
```

## Documentation page

```text
Documentation navigation → page title → short summary → prerequisites → sequential instructions → code examples → expected result → troubleshooting → related documentation
```

Optimize for scanning with stable anchors, constrained prose width, and copyable technical examples.

## Dashboard list page

```text
Page title → primary action → filters or search → optional summary or status → table or structured list → pagination or loading → empty state → error state
```

Prefer tables for comparable records. Keep the main action visible. Cards need a meaningful interaction boundary.

## Record-detail page

```text
Record identity and status → primary actions → key facts → main content → activity or related records → applicable result states
```

## Settings or form page

```text
Page title → scope explanation → grouped fields → inline help → validation → save or submit → separated destructive actions
```

Keep labels visible. A one-column form is the default unless users must compare values. Destructive controls remain distinct without competing with routine save behavior.

## Authentication page

```text
Product identity → authentication form → recovery path → required legal or policy links
```

A compact centered composition is acceptable. Keep decoration minimal and preserve keyboard operation or screen-reader support.

## Empty state

```text
State description → reason or context → one next action → optional compact detail
```

Keep the message brief and the action specific. Large illustrations and several competing actions obscure the recovery path.

## Error state

```text
Plain-language problem → useful cause or context → recovery action → optional support or diagnostic reference
```

Preserve user input and safe retry behavior where possible.

## Component or application feature

Use for a focused change inside an established interface.

```text
Purpose and surrounding context → information hierarchy → primary interaction → control states → result states → keyboard and screen-reader behavior → responsive behavior within the parent
```

Control states cover applicable behavior from this set:

```text
default | hover | focus | active | disabled
```

Result states use the same rule:

```text
loading | empty | success | error
```

Match surrounding tokens and components; one feature cannot introduce a new visual system.

# Frontend Task Brief

Complete this working brief before implementation. Keep each answer concrete and short.

| Field | Required answer |
|---|---|
| Change | User-visible result |
| Context mode | Existing system, partial system, greenfield, or ambiguous |
| Page archetype | One selection from `page-archetypes.md` |
| User and purpose | Who uses the interface and why |
| Primary task | Result the user must be able to produce |
| Primary action | Single most important action |
| Secondary action | At most one adjacent action, when needed |
| Required content | Information needed to understand the page, make a choice, or act |
| Product evidence | Product interface, real data, code sample, terminal output, technical diagram, workflow diagram, or product-specific illustration |
| Existing system | Layouts, components, named variants, and semantic tokens to reuse |
| Missing capability | Required design-system behavior that does not exist yet |
| Responsive behavior | Reading order and action priority at each target width |
| Accessibility | Applicable keyboard, screen-reader, contrast, focus, touch-target, or reduced-motion requirement |
| Acceptance checks | Repository scripts for linting, compilation, behavior, accessibility, and visual tests |

Account for applicable states in one line:

```text
default | hover | focus | active | selected | disabled | loading | empty | success | error
```

Resolve each missing design-system capability before introducing feature-specific styling. End by reviewing the final render against `visual-review-rubric.md`.

# Frontend Standards

## Operating principle

A strong interface reveals its product and follows one visual system. It stays restrained, reads clearly, and helps users act. Real screens or data should explain the product whenever possible. Code and workflows offer further evidence; product terminology anchors that evidence in context. Build hierarchy with scale and spacing, then reinforce it through weight or alignment.

## Design-system modes

| Mode | Required behavior |
|---|---|
| Existing system | Use established components, named variants, semantic tokens, the approved icon family, and current motion conventions. |
| Partial system | Preserve every established convention. Add only the semantic token or reusable primitive the task lacks, using the project's styling layer. |
| Greenfield | Define a small semantic foundation before composing a page. |

A greenfield foundation needs neutral surfaces and text, one brand accent, semantic status colors, named type and spacing roles, a small radius set, one elevation approach or none, one icon family, plus explicit focus and motion behavior. Page-local values need a reusable name and owner before use.

## Typography

Use one UI font family. Reserve monospace for source code and commands. It also fits terminal output or fixed-width data. Paths and identifiers may warrant it when their exact form matters.

Use named roles:

```text
caption
small
body
lead
subheading
section-heading
page-heading
```

A practical greenfield scale is:

```text
caption          12 / 16
small            14 / 20
body             16 / 24
lead             18 / 28
subheading       24 / 32
section-heading  32 / 40
page-heading     40-56 / 1.05-1.15
```

Write sentence-case text and let headings wrap naturally. Keep prose near 60 to 72 characters per line. Use regular body weight and 600 or 700 for headings or strong emphasis; limit the interface to three weights. Centered paragraphs should remain short enough to fit within two lines.

## Layout

Left alignment is the default. Centering fits authentication panels and compact empty, confirmation, or approved call-to-action regions.

Use named container roles such as `prose`, `content`, `page`, and `wide`. A practical greenfield spacing scale is:

```text
4  8  12  16  24  32  48  64  96
```

A section needs a clear purpose and one coherent content group. Give it a visible heading when context requires one. Consistent vertical spacing should expose the reading order. Empty space earns its place by improving readability or grouping.

## Visual tokens

Use neutral surface and text scales with one brand accent. Status colors should map to success, warning, danger, or information. Application code consumes semantic tokens instead of raw literals.

Choose one approved elevation system or omit shadows. Functional boundaries must remain legible without decorative effects. Use project radius tokens; a practical greenfield set is `4px`, `8px`, and `12px`. Full pills belong to tags, status chips, avatars, toggles, or compact segmented controls. Primary controls use the normal component radius.

## Icons and motion

Use one approved icon family with fixed sizes and consistent stroke weights. An icon communicates meaning but does not replace a clear label. Designed icons replace emoji in interface controls.

Motion can explain state change, navigation, expansion, collapse, reordering, loading progress, or direct manipulation. Respect reduced-motion preferences. Motion must not delay content access.

## Controls and state

A visual region gets one primary action with at most one adjacent secondary action. Labels name both operation and object, as in `Install CLI`, `Create project`, `Invite teammate`, or `View documentation`.

A card should create a useful boundary, group related information, or act as an interactive unit. Plain layout often needs less chrome. Dividers or tables can supply the boundary; spacing can handle grouping.

Account for each state the feature can enter:

```text
default | hover | focus | active | selected | disabled | loading | empty | success | error
```

A state change must remain understandable without color alone.

## Accessibility

Use semantic elements with associated labels and logical reading order. Preserve keyboard operation and visible focus. Touch targets must remain usable, screen-reader names clear, and contrast compliant with WCAG AA. Reduced motion or script failure must not hide content or recovery actions.

## Responsive behavior

Review these viewports when tooling permits:

```text
390 x 844
768 x 1024
1440 x 900
```

Preserve reading order and action priority. Keep heading hierarchy and table usability intact. Form labels, touch targets, and required content must also survive each reflow. Adapt the composition deliberately instead of shrinking its desktop form until it fits.

# Forbidden Frontend Patterns

Each pattern below requires explicit authorization in the task, an approved design specification, or an established design-system implementation. Without authorization, use the replacement shown.

## Typography

| Pattern | Required replacement |
|---|---|
| Decorative display or multiple font personalities | Established UI family with semantic weight |
| Monospaced marketing labels | UI type role; reserve monospace for technical content |
| Italic, gradient, oversized, or manually broken headings | Semantic heading role with natural wrapping |
| Uppercase, widely tracked eyebrow labels | Sentence-case context label |
| Arbitrary font sizes | Named type roles |

## Layout

| Pattern | Required replacement |
|---|---|
| Viewport-height marketing hero | Value proposition and product evidence in content-driven height |
| Centered long-form or content-heavy layout | Readable left-aligned measure |
| Empty space used as spectacle | Spacing that clarifies grouping and reading order |
| Generic feature-card row | Structure driven by the actual content |
| Repeated cards without a useful boundary | Plain layout, list, table, or divider |
| Arbitrary container width | Named container role |
| Decorative asymmetry that harms scanning | Clear alignment system |

## Effects and imagery

| Pattern | Required replacement |
|---|---|
| Decorative gradient, glow, blurred blob, glass panel, backdrop blur, grain, noise, text shadow, or neon border | Surface and type hierarchy supported by borders and spacing |
| Several shadow systems | One approved elevation scale or none |
| Orbit, star field, floating-object collage, node network, particle field, generic AI brain, robot, or cloud art | Real interface, real data, code, workflow, or product-specific diagram |
| Abstract artwork in place of evidence | Product mechanism in the archetype's required region |

## Components and styling

| Pattern | Required replacement |
|---|---|
| Pill-shaped primary button | Standard control radius |
| Emoji used as an interface icon | Approved icon with accessible label |
| One-off variant or unapproved icon library | Normal design-system review path |
| Raw control when an approved component exists | Component that already owns behavior and states |
| Custom navigation without approval | Established information architecture |
| New font import in feature code | Established font setup |
| Inline style or raw visual value | Semantic token and named variant |
| Raw CSS outside approved styling locations | Project styling layer that can govern and reuse it |

## Motion

Decorative entrances and perpetual animation need authorization. Otherwise motion exists only for feedback, continuity, progress, or direct manipulation.

## Copy

Generic transformation claims need concrete replacements:

| Generic frame | Replace with |
|---|---|
| `The future of...`, `Reimagine...`, or `Transform the way...` | Specific user and task |
| `Work smarter...` or `Unlock the power of...` | Mechanism and result |
| `Your work should compound` or `The memory that compounds` | Concrete mechanism and current result |
| `Built for the modern...` or `One platform for everything` | Current scope or constraint |

## Rejection test

Reject the design when changing the logo and product noun would make its composition and copy suitable for an unrelated software company.

# Frontend Content Standards

## Headings

A heading should identify at least one of these:

- What the page or section is
- What the user can do
- What problem the feature solves
- What result the product produces

Prefer concrete headings:

```text
Give coding agents the decisions behind your repository
Review failed inspections by job
Connect QuickBooks to JobNimbus
```

Replace broad mood claims such as these:

```text
Your work should compound
Meet the future of operations
A better way forward
```

## Supporting copy

Use concrete nouns and active verbs. Name the capability, mechanism, result, and relevant scope.

Prefer:

```text
Lore indexes architecture decisions, meeting notes, and prior agent sessions so coding agents can retrieve cited project context.
```

Replace:

```text
Lore transforms how modern teams unlock the power of collective intelligence.
```

## Buttons and links

Use specific actions:

```text
Install CLI
Connect repository
Create dashboard
Invite teammate
View API docs
```

Use a broad label such as `Get started` only when the next step is genuinely general and no precise action exists. Labels such as `Explore`, `Discover`, `Learn more`, and `Try it` need a concrete object or a more exact verb.

## Feature descriptions

Structure feature copy as:

```text
Capability
Mechanism
Result
Constraint or scope
```

Example:

```text
Retrieve prior decisions

Lore indexes repository notes and agent sessions, then returns cited context to supported coding tools. Developers can inspect each source before accepting a recommendation.
```

## Claims

Use measurable or testable claims where possible. Qualify beta behavior, planned integrations, performance estimates, and unverified outcomes. Replace absolutes such as `Never lose context again`, `Works with every tool`, or `Eliminates hallucinations` with a bounded description of current behavior.

## Interface voice

Use sentence case. Product UI should orient, report status, and name actions. Marketing copy should still identify the user, task, mechanism, or result. Remove prompt language, design commentary, and claims that could fit an unrelated product.

# Visual Review Rubric

Review every supplied wide-screen and narrow-screen render. Apply each relevant category and reject the interface for any critical failure.

## Product specificity

A passing interface visibly reflects the real product. It puts concrete evidence where the selected archetype requires it, while copy identifies a user, task, mechanism, result, or constraint.

| Rule | Failure evidence | Correction |
|---|---|---|
| `product-specificity.generic-interface` | Composition could represent an unrelated product | Replace generic regions with product-specific structure |
| `product-specificity.abstract-evidence` | Abstract decoration replaces product evidence | Show the interface, data, code, workflow, or technical diagram |
| `product-specificity.generic-copy` | Claims omit a product-specific task or mechanism | Name the user action and how the product supports it |

`product-specificity.logo-swap-test` is critical: a different logo and product noun make the interface suitable for an unrelated software company.

## Typography

A passing interface uses one UI family, reserves monospace for technical content, follows semantic roles, wraps headings naturally, and keeps body copy readable.

| Rule | Failure evidence | Correction |
|---|---|---|
| `typography.multiple-ui-fonts` | Several font personalities compete | Use the established UI family |
| `typography.decorative-heading` | Heading uses italics, gradient text, wide tracking, or manual breaks | Restore its semantic heading role |
| `typography.arbitrary-scale` | Type sizes do not form a coherent hierarchy | Map text to named roles |
| `typography.centered-long-copy` | Long prose is centered or too wide | Use a readable left-aligned measure |

## Composition

A passing composition follows its archetype. The primary task is obvious, reading order survives each viewport, and alignment or empty space clarifies groups.

| Rule | Failure evidence | Correction |
|---|---|---|
| `composition.archetype-gap` | Required region or state is absent | Add the missing functional region |
| `composition.competing-actions` | Several actions compete as primary | Establish one primary action |
| `composition.decorative-cards` | Cards fill space without useful grouping | Use plain layout, list, table, or dividers |
| `composition.mobile-order` | Narrow layout loses context or action priority | Reorder content around the primary task |
| `composition.spectacle-over-task` | Visual effect displaces product use | Center the composition on task evidence |

## Visual restraint and consistency

A passing interface gets hierarchy from scale and spacing, supported by weight, alignment, or grouping. Effects are functional and components share one token system.

| Rule | Failure evidence | Correction |
|---|---|---|
| `restraint.decorative-effects` | Gradients, glows, blobs, glass, or noise carry hierarchy | Restore semantic surfaces and typography |
| `restraint.decorative-imagery` | Generic imagery dominates product content | Replace it with concrete evidence |
| `restraint.pill-primary-control` | Primary control uses an oversized pill | Use the standard control radius |
| `restraint.multiple-systems` | Radius, shadow, border, icon, or color treatments conflict | Use the established token family |

## Content quality

Passing text uses concrete headings, controls with specific verbs and objects, explanations of mechanism or result, and qualified claims.

| Rule | Failure evidence | Correction |
|---|---|---|
| `content.generic-ai-language` | Copy relies on broad AI or transformation claims | Name the actual capability and result |
| `content.clever-over-clear` | Heading favors mood or wordplay over meaning | State the section purpose |
| `content.vague-action` | Control label is unspecific | Name the operation and object |
| `content.unqualified-claim` | Visible claim is absolute or unsupported | Bound or substantiate the claim |

## Accessibility

A passing render has readable contrast, visible keyboard focus, usable touch targets, logical order, clear control names, and motion that preserves access.

| Rule | Failure evidence | Correction |
|---|---|---|
| `accessibility.contrast` | Text or control lacks readable contrast | Use an approved accessible token pair |
| `accessibility.focus` | Supplied evidence shows no visible focus | Apply the system focus treatment |
| `accessibility.touch-target` | Control is too small or crowded for reliable touch | Increase its interactive area |
| `accessibility.label` | Control lacks a visible or inferable name | Add an associated label or accessible name |
| `accessibility.motion` | Motion hides content or ignores reduced-motion behavior | Preserve content and disable nonessential motion |

A task-critical control that cannot be perceived or operated is a critical failure.

## Responsive integrity

A passing interface keeps required content visible, adapts dense components deliberately, and does more than scale down the wide layout.

| Rule | Failure evidence | Correction |
|---|---|---|
| `responsive.clipping` | Required content clips, overlaps, or overflows | Reflow or constrain the affected region |
| `responsive.desktop-shrink` | Wide composition only shrinks | Define a narrow-layout reading order |
| `responsive.hidden-action` | Task-critical action disappears or loses context | Restore it near the relevant content |

A viewport that prevents the primary task is a critical failure.

## Result contract

Return this object:

```json
{
  "result": "pass",
  "critical_failures": [],
  "violations": [],
  "notes": []
```

# Yinshi

Yinshi is a browser-based coding environment for running [pi](https://pi.dev) agents against Git repositories. Users import a GitHub repository or an allowed local repository, create an isolated workspace branch, chat with the agent, then review the resulting branch through normal Git tooling.

## How It Works

Importing a repository stores a bare checkout on the server. Private GitHub repositories use the GitHub App integration. A workspace is a git worktree on a throwaway branch, so main stays untouched until the user merges outside Yinshi. The chat view streams pi agent events while the agent edits files inside that workspace.

Yinshi is designed for browser-first use. It removes local IDE setup, works from mobile browsers, and lets users bring their own model-provider credentials. Provider secrets are stored through AES-256-GCM encryption.

## Data Protection Model

Yinshi uses a middle-ground security model rather than zero-knowledge hosting. The server still sees plaintext while it runs user sessions. Stored user data is protected through per-user encryption keys, optional SQLCipher tenant databases, encrypted sensitive control fields, narrow sidecar container mounts, and HTTPS enforcement. See [docs/security/middle-ground-threat-model.md](docs/security/middle-ground-threat-model.md) for the exact guarantee, the non-guarantee, and operator duties.

## Architecture

The backend is FastAPI. SQLite stores data in a control database plus one tenant database per user. Pydantic handles request validation and settings. Authlib provides Google and GitHub OAuth. The `cryptography` package handles AES-256-GCM and HKDF. `slowapi` rate-limits sensitive routes. `httpx` is used for outbound HTTP calls. Uvicorn serves the ASGI app.

The frontend is React 18 with React Router, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, Vite, Vitest, and Playwright. Chat markdown rendering uses `react-markdown` with `remark-gfm`.

The sidecar is a Node.js bridge to the pi coding agent SDK. In tenant mode, the backend starts a dedicated Podman container per user and talks to the sidecar over a Unix domain socket. By default the sidecar receives only the active runtime paths it needs, not the user's whole data directory.

SQLCipher support is optional at install time. Production deployments that set `TENANT_DB_ENCRYPTION=required` must install either `sqlcipher3` or `pysqlcipher3` in the backend environment.

## Development

Backend development uses per-user containers by default. Set `CONTAINER_ENABLED=false` only for explicit no-auth, development, or test execution on the host.

```bash
cd backend
python -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
pip install -r requirements/base.txt
cp .env.example .env
uvicorn yinshi.main:app --reload
```

## Project Structure

```text
backend/
  src/yinshi/            FastAPI app, tenant DB code, auth, services, API routes
  tests/                 pytest suite
frontend/
  src/                   React app, API client, hooks, pages, components
  public/                static assets
sidecar/
  src/                   Node.js pi agent bridge
lit/
  yinshi.lit.md          annotated source document
```

## Documentation

The full annotated source is available as a literate program: [lit/yinshi.lit.md](lit/yinshi.lit.md).

Run coding agents in your browser

Yinshi makes it easy to manage coding agents across git repos and worktrees.

Get Started Architecture

Import repos from Github or your local machine. Yinshi spawns a worktree, connects a pi agent , and enables context engineering from any device, anywhere you have an internet connection.

Capabilities

Tenant Isolation

Each account runs in its own tenant boundary. Yinshi keeps per-user data separate and runs the sidecar in a dedicated container with dropped Linux capabilities, no-new-privileges, and resource limits. Private repos are supported through a GitHub App integration.

Container isolation GitHub App integration

AI Agent Sessions

Converse with a coding agent that reads, writes, and refactors code inside your workspace. Every change is tracked on its own branch - review, merge, or discard.

Mobile-First Interface

Work from anywhere. The responsive interface adapts from phone to desktop, keeping your agent sessions accessible on any device.

Encrypted Secrets

Provider keys and connection secrets are encrypted at rest with AES-256-GCM. Per-user encryption keys are wrapped using HKDF-derived key encryption keys, so stored secrets are not kept as plaintext.

Encryption and key management

No IDE or app required. Fire up your browser, import your repos and pi configs, and get to work.

Yinshi
Sign In / Sign Up

Yinshi

Run coding agents in your browser

Yinshi makes it easy to manage coding agents across git repos and worktrees.

Get Started Architecture

Import repos from Github or your local machine. Yinshi spawns a worktree, connects a pi agent , and enables context engineering from any device, anywhere you have an internet connection.

Capabilities

Tenant Isolation

Each account runs in its own tenant boundary. Yinshi keeps per-user data separate and runs the sidecar in a dedicated container with dropped Linux capabilities, no-new-privileges, and resource limits. Private repos are supported through a GitHub App integration.

Container isolation GitHub App integration

AI Agent Sessions

Converse with a coding agent that reads, writes, and refactors code inside your workspace. Every change is tracked on its own branch - review, merge, or discard.

Mobile-First Interface

Work from anywhere. The responsive interface adapts from phone to desktop, keeping your agent sessions accessible on any device.

Encrypted Secrets

Provider keys and connection secrets are encrypted at rest with AES-256-GCM. Per-user encryption keys are wrapped using HKDF-derived key encryption keys, so stored secrets are not kept as plaintext.

Encryption and key management

No IDE or app required. Fire up your browser, import your repos and pi configs, and get to work.

Get Started
Yinshi · Code with AI agents, anywhere.

export const TDD_RULES = `## TDD rules

Work in vertical Red -> Green slices. Refactoring is a separate, optional review activity performed only while relevant tests are green; never require a refactor merely to permit the next red test.

### Test quality

Tests must verify public behavior through an appropriate seam. Existing, obvious public seams may be used without interrupting the user. When multiple materially different seams exist or the public contract is unclear, require the agent to ask the user before committing to one.

A test must have an independent source of truth. Block tautological tests whose expected value repeats the implementation calculation, compares a value to itself, or otherwise cannot disagree with the production code.

Mock only system boundaries such as external APIs, clocks, randomness, or occasionally persistent stores. Block tests coupled to private methods, internal collaborators, call order, or other implementation details when public behavior can be observed instead.

### Red phase

One pending write may add at most one behavior-driving test. Test scaffolding, imports, fixtures, and restructuring existing tests do not count as another behavior.

Adding that single test is allowed without prior red evidence. Before production behavior is implemented, session evidence must show the relevant test failing for the expected reason. Syntax, import, collection, and fixture failures are not a clean red.

A missing import, symbol, or compatible signature may be resolved with the smallest placeholder needed to reach an assertion failure. A placeholder must not implement the asserted behavior.

Characterization tests that pin existing behavior may pass immediately. They do not require an artificial failure.

### Green phase

After a clean red, allow only the minimum production behavior required by that observed failure. Block speculative branches, APIs, validation, and abstractions not required by the current test.

A single behavior may need several mechanical writes. Imports, signatures, moves, and other transient states are allowed when they support the same current slice and do not add untested behavior.

### Green-only maintenance

Deletion and behavior-preserving refactoring do not require a new failing test, but relevant tests must have passed before the change. Types, interfaces, renames, constant extraction, test-helper extraction, and control-flow cleanup are allowed when they do not add behavior.

### User authority

A direct user instruction in the recent session to permit a specific change overrides this policy. Do not infer an override from the coding agent's own prose.`;

export const ACTIVE_GUARD_PROMPT = `TDD Guard is active for behavior-bearing code. Follow the tdd skill: work one vertical slice at a time, write a behavior-facing test first, observe a clean relevant failure, then add only enough production code to pass. Use edit or write for source changes; shell-based source writes are blocked. Do not weaken, evade, or disable the guard. If the public seam is obvious, state it and proceed; ask the user only when materially different seams or contracts require a choice.`;

]);

const EXCLUDED_DIRECTORY_NAMES = new Set([
  ".git",
  ".next",
  ".nuxt",
  ".venv",
  "__pycache__",
  "build",
  "coverage",
  "dist",
  "generated",
  "node_modules",
  "out",
  "target",
  "vendor",
  "venv",
]);

export function isBehaviorCodePath(filePath: string): boolean {
  if (filePath.length === 0) {
    return false;
  }

  const segments = filePath.replaceAll("\\", "/").split("/");
  if (segments.some((segment) => EXCLUDED_DIRECTORY_NAMES.has(segment.toLowerCase()))) {
    return false;
  }

  const extension = extname(filePath).toLowerCase();
  return BEHAVIOR_CODE_EXTENSIONS.has(extension);
}

Run coding agents against your repositories from any browser.

Run coding agents in your browser

Yinshi makes it easy to manage coding agents across git repos and worktrees.

Get Started Architecture

From repository to reviewable branch

  1. Connect a repository
  2. Give pi a task
  3. Review the branch

Capabilities

Tenant Isolation

Each account runs in its own tenant boundary. Yinshi keeps per-user data separate and runs the sidecar in a dedicated container with dropped Linux capabilities, no-new-privileges, and resource limits. Private repos are supported through a GitHub App integration.

Container isolation GitHub App integration

AI Agent Sessions

Converse with a coding agent that reads, writes, and refactors code inside your workspace. Every change is tracked on its own branch - review, merge, or discard.

Mobile-First Interface

Work from anywhere. The responsive interface adapts from phone to desktop, keeping your agent sessions accessible on any device.

Encrypted Secrets

Provider keys and connection secrets are encrypted at rest with AES-256-GCM. Per-user encryption keys are wrapped using HKDF-derived key encryption keys, so stored secrets are not kept as plaintext.

Encryption and key management

No IDE or app required. Fire up your browser, import your repos and pi configs, and get to work.

Sign In / Sign Up

Run coding agents against your repositories from any browser.

Run coding agents in your browser

Yinshi makes it easy to manage coding agents across git repos and worktrees.

Get Started Architecture

From repository to reviewable branch

  1. Connect a repository

    Choose a GitHub repository or an allowed local path available to the server.

  2. Give pi a task

    Yinshi creates a named worktree and streams pi’s messages, tool calls, and file edits.

  3. Review the branch

Capabilities

Tenant Isolation

Each account runs in its own tenant boundary. Yinshi keeps per-user data separate and runs the sidecar in a dedicated container with dropped Linux capabilities, no-new-privileges, and resource limits. Private repos are supported through a GitHub App integration.

Container isolation GitHub App integration

AI Agent Sessions

Converse with a coding agent that reads, writes, and refactors code inside your workspace. Every change is tracked on its own branch - review, merge, or discard.

Mobile-First Interface

Work from anywhere. The responsive interface adapts from phone to desktop, keeping your agent sessions accessible on any device.

Encrypted Secrets

Provider keys and connection secrets are encrypted at rest with AES-256-GCM. Per-user encryption keys are wrapped using HKDF-derived key encryption keys, so stored secrets are not kept as plaintext.

Encryption and key management

No IDE or app required. Fire up your browser, import your repos and pi configs, and get to work.

Get Started

arguments.text:
Browser-based coding workspace

Run coding agents against your repositories from any browser.

Import a GitHub or allowed local repository. Yinshi creates an isolated git worktree, connects a pi agent, and streams the session to your browser.

Start a workspace
Read the architecture

Workspace isolation
One git worktree per session
Agent runtime
pi coding agent
Repository access
GitHub App or allowed local path

From repository to reviewable branch

Connect a repository
Choose a GitHub repository or an allowed local path available to the server.

Give pi a task
Yinshi creates a named worktree and streams pi’s messages, tool calls, and file edits.

Review the branch
Inspect the result, then merge or discard the workspace through your existing Git tools.

Capabilities

Tenant isolation
Each account runs in its own tenant boundary. Yinshi keeps per-user data separate and runs the sidecar in a dedicated container with dropped Linux capabilities, no-new-privileges, and resource limits. Private repos are supported through a GitHub App integration.

AI agent sessions
Converse with a coding agent that reads, writes, and refactors code inside your workspace. Every change is tracked on its own branch - review, merge, or discard.

Mobile-first interface
Work from anywhere. The responsive interface adapts from phone to desktop, keeping your agent sessions accessible on any device.

Encrypted secrets
Provider keys and connection secrets are encrypted at rest with AES-256-GCM. Per-user encryption keys are wrapped using HKDF-derived key encryption keys, so stored secrets are not kept as plaintext.

No IDE or app required. Fire up your browser, import your repos and pi configs, and get to work.

content.text:
# Visual Review Rubric

Review every supplied wide-screen and narrow-screen render. Apply each relevant category and reject the interface for any critical failure.

## Product specificity

A passing interface visibly reflects the real product. It puts concrete evidence where the selected archetype requires it, while copy identifies a user, task, mechanism, result, or constraint.

| Rule | Failure evidence | Correction |
|---|---|---|
| `product-specificity.generic-interface` | Composition could represent an unrelated product | Replace generic regions with product-specific structure |
| `product-specificity.abstract-evidence` | Abstract decoration replaces product evidence | Show the interface, data, code, workflow, or technical diagram |
| `product-specificity.generic-copy` | Claims omit a product-specific task or mechanism | Name the user action and how the product supports it |

`product-specificity.logo-swap-test` is critical: a different logo and product noun make the interface suitable for an unrelated software company.

## Typography

A passing interface uses one UI family, reserves monospace for technical content, follows semantic roles, wraps headings naturally, and keeps body copy readable.

| Rule | Failure evidence | Correction |
|---|---|---|
| `typography.multiple-ui-fonts` | Several font personalities compete | Use the established UI family |
| `typography.decorative-heading` | Heading uses italics, gradient text, wide tracking, or manual breaks | Restore its semantic heading role |
| `typography.arbitrary-scale` | Type sizes do not form a coherent hierarchy | Map text to named roles |
| `typography.centered-long-copy` | Long prose is centered or too wide | Use a readable left-aligned measure |

## Composition

A passing composition follows its archetype. The primary task is obvious, reading order survives each viewport, and alignment or empty space clarifies groups.

| Rule | Failure evidence | Correction |
|---|---|---|
| `composition.archetype-gap` | Required region or state is absent | Add the missing functional region |
| `composition.competing-actions` | Several actions compete as primary | Establish one primary action |
| `composition.decorative-cards` | Cards fill space without useful grouping | Use plain layout, list, table, or dividers |
| `composition.mobile-order` | Narrow layout loses context or action priority | Reorder content around the primary task |
| `composition.spectacle-over-task` | Visual effect displaces product use | Center the composition on task evidence |

## Visual restraint and consistency

A passing interface gets hierarchy from scale and spacing, supported by weight, alignment, or grouping. Effects are functional and components share one token system.

| Rule | Failure evidence | Correction |
|---|---|---|
| `restraint.decorative-effects` | Gradients, glows, blobs, glass, or noise carry hierarchy | Restore semantic surfaces and typography |
| `restraint.decorative-imagery` | Generic imagery dominates product content | Replace it with concrete evidence |
| `restraint.pill-primary-control` | Primary control uses an oversized pill | Use the standard control radius |
| `restraint.multiple-systems` | Radius, shadow, border, icon, or color treatments conflict | Use the established token family |

## Content quality

Passing text uses concrete headings, controls with specific verbs and objects, explanations of mechanism or result, and qualified claims.

| Rule | Failure evidence | Correction |
|---|---|---|
| `content.generic-ai-language` | Copy relies on broad AI or transformation claims | Name the actual capability and result |
| `content.clever-over-clear` | Heading favors mood or wordplay over meaning | State the section purpose |
| `content.vague-action` | Control label is unspecific | Name the operation and object |
| `content.unqualified-claim` | Visible claim is absolute or unsupported | Bound or substantiate the claim |

## Accessibility

A passing render has readable contrast, visible keyboard focus, usable touch targets, logical order, clear control names, and motion that preserves access.

| Rule | Failure evidence | Correction |
|---|---|---|
| `accessibility.contrast` | Text or control lacks readable contrast | Use an approved accessible token pair |
| `accessibility.focus` | Supplied evidence shows no visible focus | Apply the system focus treatment |
| `accessibility.touch-target` | Control is too small or crowded for reliable touch | Increase its interactive area |
| `accessibility.label` | Control lacks a visible or inferable name | Add an associated label or accessible name |
| `accessibility.motion` | Motion hides content or ignores reduced-motion behavior | Preserve content and disable nonessential motion |

A task-critical control that cannot be perceived or operated is a critical failure.

## Responsive integrity

A passing interface keeps required content visible, adapts dense components deliberately, and does more than scale down the wide layout.

| Rule | Failure evidence | Correction |
|---|---|---|
| `responsive.clipping` | Required content clips, overlaps, or overflows | Reflow or constrain the affected region |
| `responsive.desktop-shrink` | Wide composition only shrinks | Define a narrow-layout reading order |
| `responsive.hidden-action` | Task-critical action disappears or loses context | Restore it near the relevant content |

A viewport that prevents the primary task is a critical failure.

## Result contract

Return this object:

```json
{
  "result": "pass",
  "critical_failures": [],
  "violations": [],
  "notes": []
}
```

Every finding names a rule, cites visible evidence, and identifies the affected viewport or state. Each non-critical violation includes a concrete correction. Set `result` to `fail` whenever either findings array contains an item.
